6. Data Packets: How Data Travels in Small Pieces

When you send a photo or open a web page, the data does not travel as one big lump. Instead, the network breaks it into many small pieces called data packets. This is one of the most important ideas about how the internet works.

concepts.title: Getting Online: How Devices Connect Without Wires
concepts.explanation:
There are many ways to get online — at home, at school, or outside. The most convenient way is usually wirelessly, because there are no cables to plug in and your device stays portable (easy to carry around). Phones, tablets, laptops and PCs all connect this way. Even some washing machines, fridges and watches can now connect to the internet!

So how does data travel through the air with no wires? The answer is radio waves. Your device turns your data into binary (a stream of 0s and 1s) and sends it as invisible radio waves to another device or to a mast. The other device catches those waves and turns them back into data. The three most popular wireless methods are Wi-Fi, Bluetooth and cellular data. Each one is good at different jobs.

The four things that make each method different

Whenever you compare wireless methods, engineers look at four characteristics. These four ideas are the key to the whole topic, so learn them well:

Bandwidth — how much data can be sent in a certain time. High bandwidth is needed for big jobs like streaming video. When a video keeps stopping to load (you see the spinning 'buffering' circle), it usually means there is not enough bandwidth for all that data.

Transmission distance — how far the signal can reach. You have probably walked too far from a Wi-Fi router and watched your connection drop. That is transmission distance in action.

Security — how easy it is for a hacker to break in. Some methods are much easier to attack than others, so security matters a lot when the data is private.

Interference — anything that interrupts the signal. This could be a wall, or another electronic device. A microwave oven, for example, gives off radio waves that can knock a laptop off its Wi-Fi.

We measure the amount of data sent in bits per second (bps). Because modern connections are fast, we use bigger units: kilobits (Kbps) are thousands of bits, megabits (Mbps) are millions, and gigabits (Gbps) are billions of bits per second. Every year, new versions of these technologies get faster and reach further.

Before 3G, 4G and 5G existed, the fastest mobile connection was only about 114 Kbps. At that speed, downloading one HD film would have taken more than five days! Today, 5G can do the same job in seconds.

Comparing Wi-Fi, Bluetooth and cellular data

Here is how the three methods compare. Notice how each one is a trade-off — none is 'best' at everything. Choosing the right one depends on the job:

Wi-Fi is fast (up to about 9.6 Gbps) but only reaches around 50 metres indoors — enough for one home, school or office. Its security is fairly weak: anyone in range can see the network, and passwords can be attacked. Walls, microwaves and TVs can interfere with it. Wi-Fi is perfect for connecting laptops and phones inside a building.

Bluetooth is much slower (Bluetooth 5 reaches about 2 Mbps) and only reaches around 40 metres, working best when the two devices can 'see' each other with nothing in between. Its security is also weak. Bluetooth is ideal for connecting nearby devices that do not need much data — wireless headphones, a keyboard, a mouse, or sharing a photo between two phones.
concepts.example: Cellular data comes from phone masts and lets you connect almost anywhere outdoors. 4G averages 8–10 Mbps and can reach up to 16 kilometres from a mast. 5G is much faster (around 100 Mbps) but reaches a shorter distance (about 500 metres), so cities need many more 5G masts. Security for both 4G and 5G is excellent. When Nora checks the news on her phone while walking through Kismayo, she is using cellular data.

concepts.title: Where Websites Live: Servers
concepts.explanation:
When you open a website, watch a video, or read a message, you are actually opening files that are stored on a server. A server is a powerful computer that stores files and shares them with other devices. It works just like the files on your own phone — except a server's files can be reached over the internet by people all around the world.

Servers are built for speed and storage, and they are usually stacked together in racks. Hundreds or even thousands of servers may sit together in one building called a server farm. A server that stores web pages is called a web server. To put a website online, a person called an administrator saves the website's files onto the web server. After that, anyone can view the site by typing its address into a web browser.
concepts.example: Tim Berners-Lee invented the World Wide Web in 1989. The internet was first created so that scientists at different universities could share their research automatically. It grew into the web we all use today.

concepts.title: IP Addresses: Every Device Has an Address
concepts.explanation:
Imagine sending a letter with no address on the envelope — it would never arrive. Devices on a network have the same problem, so every device is given an IP address. IP stands for Internet Protocol. An IP address is a unique number that identifies one device on a network, so other devices know exactly where to send data. Think of it as the device's 'home address'.

A common type of IP address is made of four numbers separated by full stops, and each number is between 0 and 255. For example:

On a home network, every device gets its own unique IP address. In many homes the addresses start with 192.168.1. — for example, the laptop might be 192.168.1.2, the phone 192.168.1.3, and a smart lightbulb 192.168.1.5. If a device wants to send data to the lightbulb, it uses the number 192.168.1.5, not the name 'lightbulb' — because two devices could share the same name, but IP addresses are unique, so there is never any confusion.

Servers work exactly the same way. Every web server on the internet has its own IP address so it can be found. When you understand IP addresses, you understand how one device out of billions can be located precisely.
concepts.example: "An IP address like 256.1.1.1 is fine." It is not! Each number must be between 0 and 255. So 256 is too big, and an address is invalid. An address also needs exactly four numbers — 69.171.224 is invalid because it only has three. You will practise spotting invalid addresses in your Activities.

concepts.title: URLs: Names Are Easier Than Numbers
concepts.explanation:
Could you remember the IP address of 20 different websites? Probably not — numbers like 172.217.169.78 are hard to recall. That is why we use URLs. A URL (Uniform Resource Locator) is the web address you type into your browser, and it is far easier to remember than a string of numbers.

A URL is written in a set way, and each part has a job. Look at this example and the labels below it:

https — the protocol, the set of rules for sending the data. The 's' means it is the secure version (more on that soon).

www — tells the browser you want the World Wide Web part of the site.

africanews.com — the domain name, the easy-to-remember name of the website. This is the part that changes for each different site.

.com — the top-level domain (TLD), the ending of the domain name.
concepts.example: There are over 1000 TLDs you can buy, but the most common is .com (for commercial businesses). Others include .org (organisations), .net (networks), and country endings like .ng (Nigeria), .eg (Egypt), .ae (United Arab Emirates), .in (India) and .au (Australia). When you see a TLD, you can often guess something about the website just from its ending.

concepts.title: DNS: The Internet's Phone Book
concepts.explanation:
Here is the clever bit. You type a URL (a name), but devices find each other using IP addresses (numbers). So how does the name get turned into the number? The answer is DNS, the Domain Name System.

DNS is like the contacts list in a phone. When you want to call your friend Talia, you do not remember her phone number — you just tap her name, and the phone looks up the number for you. DNS does the same for websites: it stores a giant database that matches every URL to its IP address. A small part of such a list might look like this: google.com is 209.85.231.104, and micropython.org is 176.58.119.26.

What happens when you type a URL — step by step

Imagine Sami types www.africanews.com into his browser in Mogadishu. Picture the journey of his request like this. (Try to 'see' each arrow in your mind — this is the diagram in words.)

Sami types the URL www.africanews.com into his web browser and presses Enter.

The browser sends the name to a DNS server and asks: "What is the IP address for this website?"

The DNS server looks in its database, finds the match (for example, 81.92.228.150), and sends that IP address back to Sami's computer.

If the DNS server cannot find the name, it passes the question up to a higher-level DNS — a bigger DNS with an even larger list.

If no DNS anywhere can find the name, the browser shows a 'server not found' error message, and the page does not load.

Once the browser has the IP address, it sends a request to that web server. The web server sends the web page back, and it appears on Sami's screen.

All of this normally happens in the blink of an eye. That entire lookup usually takes only 20 to 120 milliseconds — far faster than you can click your fingers.
concepts.example: A 404 error is the most famous error on the web. It means the web server was reached, but the exact page could not be found — often because of a typing mistake in the address, or because the page was moved or deleted. If the website name itself does not exist, you get a different 'server not found' message instead.

concepts.title: Data Packets: How Data Travels in Small Pieces
concepts.explanation:
When you send a photo or open a web page, the data does not travel as one big lump. Instead, the network breaks it into many small pieces called data packets. This is one of the most important ideas about how the internet works.

Think of it like this. Imagine Leila wants to send her friend a long handwritten story, but she can only use small envelopes. She tears the story into pages, puts each page in its own envelope, and writes on every envelope: the destination address, her own return address, and a page number so the pages can be put back in order. Data packets work exactly the same way.

A large piece of data is split into many small packets.

Each packet carries a piece of the data, the sender's IP address, the destination IP address, and a sequence number (its 'page number').

The packets travel across the network, and they may even take different routes to reach the same place.

At the destination, the device uses the sequence numbers to reassemble the packets back into the original data, in the correct order.

If a packet gets lost or damaged on the way, the receiver notices a piece is missing and asks for that packet to be sent again.
concepts.example: Breaking data into packets is smart because it means many people can share the same network at once, and a single damaged packet does not ruin the whole message — only that one small piece needs re-sending. This links directly to the next big idea: how errors happen and how we check that a message arrived correctly.

concepts.title: Web Browsers: Your Window to the Web
concepts.explanation:
A web browser is the program you use to view web pages — for example Firefox (which is free and open-source), Chrome, Edge or Safari. When you request a page, the browser uses DNS to find it, fetches the files from the web server, and displays them in its display window.

Every browser looks a little different, but they all share the same key parts: an address bar where you type the URL, and navigation buttons (back, forward and refresh) to move between pages. Browsers also let you bookmark pages you want to find again later.

Here is an important idea for the whole Computing course: a web browser is a type of application software. Application software is a program built to do one particular job for the user. A browser's one job is to browse the World Wide Web — so it is application software, just like a calculator app or a word processor.

8. Is This Website Safe? HTTPS, Padlocks and Certificates

Some websites handle very private information — passwords, messages, or payment details. Others just show public information, like a list of match results. Websites that handle private data must protect it, and your browser gives you clues to check whether a site is protected.

The padlock icon. A small padlock next to the address means the connection is encrypted and the site has an SSL certificate proving it is genuine. You can click the padlock to see more details about the site's security.

The https at the start of the URL. The 's' stands for 'secure'. HTTPS is the secure protocol: any data sent between your browser and the website is scrambled so that hackers cannot read it. A plain http address (with no 's') is not secure.

An SSL certificate is a digital certificate that does two jobs: it proves the website owner is genuine, and it lets the connection use encryption. When a site has one, everything sent between the web server and your browser — including anything you type — is encrypted (scrambled) before it is sent, and decrypted (unscrambled) when it arrives. If a hacker managed to grab the data on the way, it would just look like nonsense.

How strong is this protection? The encryption used by a site like google.com would take modern computers around 500 billion years to break without the key. That is why you can shop and bank online safely — as long as you check for the padlock and https first.

Checking a certificate for real

You can go further than just looking for the padlock. If you click the padlock, you can view the certificate itself and see who issued it — the trusted organisation that confirmed the site is genuine. For example, the certificate for micropython.org was issued by an authority called 'R3'. You can also visit a website such as who.is to look up who owns a domain name, which usually shows a contact address for the owner.

"If there is a padlock, the website is completely safe and I can trust it." Be careful. The padlock only means the connection is encrypted — that nobody can spy on the data as it travels. It does NOT promise the website itself is honest. A dishonest website can still have a padlock. Always think about who runs a site before you trust it with your information.
concepts.example: There is one more warning. Even a site that shows SSL and HTTPS is not automatically safe if your own computer has a virus. A virus could trick your browser into thinking a site is secure when it is not. This is why you should keep your device protected and never ignore security warnings.

concepts.title: Encryption: Turning Messages Into Secret Code
concepts.explanation:
Messages sent across a network can be intercepted (secretly captured) on the way. If a message is sent as ordinary plaintext, anyone who captures it can read it. Imagine Computer 1 sending the message "Your password is: aXa1239" in plaintext — a hacker who grabbed it would see the password immediately.

Encryption solves this. It scrambles the message into cipher text that looks like nonsense, such as "JHAF&^-FDJG". The message can still be intercepted, but now the hacker cannot understand it. Only the device with the correct key can decrypt it back into readable plaintext. To encrypt data, the two devices agree on an algorithm (a set of steps) so the receiver knows how to unscramble the message.

One famous, simple cipher is the Caesar cipher. It works by shifting the alphabet along by a fixed number of places. In this book, a shift of two moves each letter two places to the left in the alphabet — so the letter A becomes Y, B becomes Z, C becomes A, and so on. The top row is the plaintext; the bottom row is the cipher text you write instead.

To encrypt, you find each plaintext letter in the top row and write the letter below it. To decrypt, you do the opposite. Using the shift-of-two table, the word HELLO would encrypt to FCJJM. You will practise encrypting and decrypting in your Activities booklet.
concepts.example: A simple substitution cipher is similar, but instead of a neat shift, every letter is swapped for another letter at random. To decode it, you need the full swap list. For example, with one such list the plaintext HELLO becomes PBOOR. A random substitution is harder to crack than a plain shift, because there is no simple pattern to guess.

concepts.title: When Data Goes Wrong: Errors in Transmission
concepts.explanation:
Computers talk to each other in binary — streams of bits (0s and 1s). A group of 8 bits is called a byte, and one byte often stands for a single character. Sometimes, while data is travelling, a bit can get corrupted — it flips from a 1 to a 0, or a 0 to a 1 — and this causes an error.

There are several reasons errors happen when data is sent:

Power surges — a sudden jump in electrical power, often caused by lightning.

Broken or damaged cables — a faulty wire can scramble the signal.

Electrical interference — many electronic devices close together can disturb each other's signals.

Hacking — someone deliberately interfering with the data.

Here is a real example. Computer 1 wants to send the byte 01000101. But the receiving computer has a faulty cable, so Computer 2 receives 00000101 instead. Look carefully: the second bit flipped from a 1 to a 0. That tiny change is an error, and it could turn one character into a completely different one.
concepts.example: This is exactly why data packets carry checking information. The receiving device can detect that something arrived wrongly and ask for that packet to be sent again. Error checking is how the internet stays reliable even though mistakes happen all the time.

concepts.title: Search Engines and Artificial Intelligence
concepts.explanation:
A search engine is a website that searches other websites for you. It keeps a huge database of web pages. When you type a query, it returns a list of pages that match. Google's database holds over 35 trillion web pages!

Search engines work by picking out keywords. You do not need to write full sentences — if Rohan types "Show me the latest game consoles", the search engine ignores the extra words and focuses on the keywords game consoles. Knowing this helps you search better: choose clear, important keywords.

Search engines now use machine learning and artificial intelligence to give better results. Here are three ways:

Learning from people. Every time users search for something, the search engine remembers which page they actually wanted, and moves that page higher up the list for the next person. Over time, the results get more and more accurate.

Using your location. If someone in Cairo searches for 'bicycle repair shops', the results show shops in the Cairo area, not the other side of the world.

Searching with pictures. You can now search using an image instead of words — this is called a reverse image search.

Reverse image search and neural networks

In a reverse image search, you upload a digitised image (a picture stored as a computer file, such as a JPEG or PNG). The computer uses image recognition: it studies the picture's distinctive points, colours, lines and textures, then compares them against billions of images in its database. When it finds close matches, it shows them to you. In one famous example, a search not only recognised a photo as a helicopter, but even identified the exact model — a 'Bell 206'.

The technology behind this often uses a neural network — a type of machine learning designed to work a little like the human brain. The more people use it, the more examples it learns from, and the more accurate it becomes. With around 5.6 billion searches every day, a big search engine has an enormous amount to learn from.

Machine learning has created brand-new kinds of apps. For example, there are apps that let you photograph a plant, an animal or an object, and the app instantly tells you what it is — all by recognising the image.

Staying Safe and Responsible Online

Understanding how the internet works also means understanding how to use it safely and kindly. You already value trust, honesty and respecting other people's privacy — and these same values make you a safe and responsible person online. Here is how to put them into practice:

Guard your private information. Never share your full name, home address, school, phone number or passwords with people you do not know online.

Use strong, private passwords. A strong password is long and mixes letters, numbers and symbols. Never share it — not even with a friend. Use a different password for important accounts.

Check before you trust. Look for https and the padlock before typing any private information into a website, especially on an online shop.

Be trustworthy with others' data. If a friend shares something private with you, keep it private. Do not spread other people's information or photos without permission.

Think before you type. Be kind and honest in messages. Words online can be saved and shared — write only what you would be happy for anyone to read.
concepts.example: Ask a trusted adult if something online worries you, scares you, or does not feel right. You are never in trouble for asking.

esafety.title: Keep personal information private
esafety.text: Your full name, address, school, phone number, birthday and passwords are personal information. Never type them into a game, an app or a website, and never send them to someone you only know online.

esafety.title: Check before you trust
esafety.text: Anyone can put anything on the internet, so not everything you read is true. Check an important fact on a second, different website, and ask an adult you trust if you are not sure.

esafety.title: Tell someone if something worries you
esafety.text: If anything online upsets you, or someone asks you for personal information or to keep a secret, stop, leave the page and tell an adult you trust straight away. It is never your fault.

esafety.title: Respect other people's work
esafety.text: Pictures, music and writing belong to whoever made them. Use work that is free to use, and say where you got it. Your own work belongs to you — put your name on it.

rules.title: ! — DNS in one line
rules.text: DNS is the internet's phone book: you give it a name (URL), it gives you back a number (IP address) so your browser can find the website.

rules.title: ! — Check before you type
rules.text: Before entering any private information, look for the padlock and https, and make sure you trust the website. The padlock protects the connection, not your judgement.

rules.title: ! — Packets and errors
rules.text: Data travels in small packets. If a packet is damaged or lost, only that packet is re-sent. That is how the internet stays reliable even when errors happen.

rules.title: ! — A browser is application software
rules.text: A web browser does one specific job — browsing the World Wide Web — so it is a type of application software.

terms: connectivity
The way devices connect to each other to form a network.
network
A group of computers and devices connected so they can share data.
the internet
The huge global network that connects billions of devices worldwide.
Wi-Fi
A wireless method of connecting devices using radio waves, over a short range.
Bluetooth
A wireless method for connecting nearby devices using radio waves.
cellular data
Mobile internet from phone masts, such as 4G and 5G.
bandwidth
The amount of data that can be sent in a certain amount of time.
transmission distance
How far a signal can travel using a transmission method.
interference
Anything that interrupts a signal, such as walls or other devices.
server
A powerful computer that stores and manages files and services for a network.
web server
A server that stores web pages so people can view them online.
IP address
A unique number that identifies a device on a network, e.g. 192.168.1.4.
URL
A web address you type into a browser, e.g. https://www.africanews.com.
domain name
The easy-to-remember part of a URL, e.g. africanews.com.
DNS
Domain Name System — it translates a URL into an IP address.
data packet
A small chunk of data with address labels, used to send data across a network.
web browser
Application software used to find and display web pages.
protocol
A set of rules for how devices send data to each other.
HTTPS
The secure protocol for sending web data; shown as https in the address bar.
encryption
Scrambling data with a key so only the right device can read it.
SSL certificate
A digital certificate proving a website is genuine and uses encryption.
padlock icon
A symbol in the address bar showing the connection is encrypted (HTTPS).
404 error
An error message shown in a browser when a page cannot be found.
plaintext
A message before it is encrypted — one that can be read easily.
